content.title: Gas prices may ease after Iran ceasefire, but relief could take time
content.text: SALINE COUNTY, Ark. (KATV) — EMS Week in Saline County is shining a spotlight on first responders while drawing attention to the mental health challenges that come with the job.A new partnership tied to this year’s events aims to break the stigma surrounding mental health and connect emergency crews with support and resources.During a recent ride-along, paramedic and operations supervisor Preston Freeman with Pafford EMS described the unpredictable nature of the work, where routine moments can quickly turn into emergencies.“The day doesn’t start with an emergency, but it can turn into one at any moment,” Freeman said.Between calls, supervisors check on crews stationed across the county to make sure they are prepared for whatever comes next. But once a call comes in, the pace shifts instantly, often requiring split-second decisions under pressure.Freeman said even driving to a scene presents risks.“Who’s going to hit me? It really is, because drivers are so unpredictable,” he said.Inside the ambulance, that pressure continues.“We’ve got very highly trained individuals who know what they’re doing. They know how to work under pressure. They thrive under pressure, but it is also managed chaos,” Freeman said.This year’s EMS Week also carries a deeper meaning, honoring firefighter and EMT Brittany Wildhaber, who died by suicide. Organizers said her death is a reminder of the emotional toll the job can take.Freeman said certain calls, especially involving children, can be difficult to process.“All of my kid calls stick with me just because they’re a young life, and they haven’t gotten to experience any life,” he said. “It’s always a tragedy when anything like that happens.”To cope, crews often rely on one another, talking through calls and decompressing together after difficult situations.“They all go around it, talk, decompress, kind of run through, ‘Hey, this is what we had. This is what we saw. What’d y’all think? Did I miss anything?’” Freeman said.Still, the stress is constant. Many EMS workers remain on shift for extended periods, carrying that pressure even while trying to rest.“You’re sitting around in a high-stress environment constantly,” Freeman said. “We stay here for 48 hours. So you sleep with that on your mind. You go to bed wondering, ‘When am I going to get woken up? What’s it going to be?’”Organizers said EMS Week events will focus on providing support, sharing resources and encouraging open conversations about mental health.Comment with BubblesBE THE FIRST TO COMMENTCommunity members are encouraged to participate and show support for local EMS crews.
